lessons.title: Meet JavaScript
lessons.subtitle: A little code. A whole new world of possibilities.
lessons.objective: Explain what JavaScript does, where it runs, and how it works with HTML and CSS.
lessons.why: A document can show information. A program can respond to information. JavaScript gives websites instructions for responding to people and changing data.
lessons.real: When a shopping cart updates its total without reloading the page, browser JavaScript can update the interface. A server still checks prices, stock, and payment.
lessons.analogy: Think of a café: HTML is the building and menu, CSS is the décor, and JavaScript is the staff responding to your order.

sections.title: Three languages, one experience
sections.text: HTML describes structure: headings, inputs, and buttons. CSS controls presentation: color, spacing, and layout. JavaScript adds general-purpose behavior and logic: checking an answer, calculating a total, or changing text after a click. HTML and CSS offer some built-in interactions, but do not replace general-purpose programming.

sections.title: A small beginning, a big reach
sections.text: Brendan Eich created JavaScript in 1995 at Netscape to add scripting to web pages. It later became standardized as ECMAScript. JavaScript and Java are different languages; their similar names do not mean their syntax or runtime is the same.

sections.title: Where does the code run?
sections.text: A browser contains a JavaScript engine: a program that reads and executes your instructions. The browser also provides APIs (ready-made tools) for the page, clicks, and timers. Node.js runs JavaScript outside the browser, often on a server. A server is a computer that responds to requests from other computers.

sections.title: JavaScript, Python, PHP, and Java
sections.text: Browser JavaScript runs in the visitor’s browser. PHP commonly runs on a server and generates responses such as HTML. JavaScript can also run on servers using Node.js. Python is widely used for automation, data work, and servers; Java is used in many server and enterprise systems. These languages overlap in capability and are chosen for different contexts. PHP is actively used, not obsolete.

sections.title: Power comes with boundaries
sections.text: JavaScript is built into browsers and responds quickly to user input. Its flexible types can also cause surprising conversions. Browser code cannot freely read your computer’s files, and visible client code must never contain secret passwords. Long-running code can block an interface; our practice runner uses a separate worker with a time limit.

examples.title: Give the browser an instruction
examples.code: console.log("Hello, curious human!");
examples.explanation: console.log sends a message to the console, a window into what your program is doing. The quoted text is a string.

examples.title: Let JavaScript calculate
examples.code:
console.log(149 + 51);
console.log("Items in cart:", 2);
examples.explanation: Numbers can be added. A comma lets console.log display several values on one line.

examples.title: Change what people see
examples.code: document.getElementById("message").textContent = "You made this happen!";
examples.explanation: The DOM is the browser’s representation of a page. getElementById finds a page element; textContent changes its text. The lab provides a small simulated preview with a message element.

predict.explanation: Without quotes, 3 and 7 are numbers. The + operator adds them.

debug.prompt: This message is missing a closing quote. Repair it and run the code.
debug.hint: Strings need matching quotes at both ends.

challenge.prompt: Introduce yourself in the console, then print the number of students in a class of 12 + 8.
challenge.starter: // Print a greeting and the class total
challenge.solution:
console.log("Hello! I am learning JavaScript.");
console.log(12 + 8);
challenge.hint: Use one console.log for text in quotes and another for the calculation.

quiz.prompt: Which language describes the structure of a page?
quiz.explanation: HTML describes elements such as headings, paragraphs, and buttons.

quiz.prompt: JavaScript can run on a server.
quiz.explanation: Node.js is a runtime that executes JavaScript outside the browser, including on servers.

quiz.prompt: A cart total changes after you add an item. Which role fits JavaScript?
quiz.explanation: JavaScript can respond to a click and calculate a displayed total. The backend still validates purchases.

lessons.summary: HTML gives a page structure. CSS gives it style. JavaScript gives it behavior and logic. It runs in browsers and in other runtimes such as Node.js.

notes.say: A website can listen, decide, and respond. JavaScript describes those instructions.
notes.demo: Toggle HTML, CSS, and JavaScript one at a time. Click the preview button after each change.
notes.ask: Does a yellow button automatically know what to do when clicked?
notes.answer: No. CSS controls its appearance. JavaScript can attach the behavior.
notes.misconception: JavaScript is not Java, and it is not limited to browsers.
notes.exercise: Ask pairs to name one structure, one style, and one behavior on a food ordering website.
notes.transition: Now that we know what JavaScript does, let’s give it our first instruction.

lessons.title: Your first program
lessons.subtitle: Turn an idea into your very first instruction.
lessons.objective: Write and run statements, understand console output, and update text on a page.
lessons.why: Programs are sequences of instructions. Output helps us see whether those instructions are doing what we intended.
lessons.real: Developers use the console to inspect values and diagnose bugs. Websites update DOM text to show a cart count or a welcome message.
lessons.analogy: The console is like a kitchen order window: you send out a message so someone can see what is happening inside.

sections.title: Your browser has a workshop
sections.text: Open developer tools with F12 or Ctrl+Shift+J (Cmd+Option+J on macOS in Chrome), then choose Console. Browser shortcuts vary. The console accepts JavaScript and displays results and errors. The editor below gives you a classroom console without leaving this site.

sections.title: Statements, comments, and punctuation
sections.text: A statement is one instruction. Parentheses pass information into a function, a reusable action. Quoted text is a string. Semicolons explicitly end statements; JavaScript can insert many automatically, but we use them for clarity. // begins a one-line comment that the engine ignores.
sections.code:
// This explains the next instruction
console.log("Hello World!");

sections.title: Inside HTML or in a separate file
sections.text: An internal script goes inside a script element. An external script uses src to load a .js file. defer lets an external script run after the HTML is parsed. The following is HTML setup, not code to paste into our JavaScript-only runner.
sections.code:
<script>console.log("Internal script");</script>
<script src="app.js" defer></script>

sections.title: Different ways to communicate
sections.text: console.log writes developer output. alert normally shows a blocking browser dialog. prompt normally asks for text and returns a string, or null if cancelled. Our isolated runner displays alert messages in the console and uses the editable prompt response field instead of opening dialogs.
sections.code:
let name = prompt("What is your name?");
alert("Hello, " + name);

sections.title: Updating the page safely
sections.text: document.write inserts HTML while a document is loading. Calling it later can replace the page, so modern apps generally avoid it. Use DOM methods and textContent for text updates. Our preview simulates just getElementById("message").textContent and document.write for this introduction; it is not a complete browser DOM.

examples.title: Hello, console
examples.explanation: The first line prints a greeting. The second calculates 30 before printing it. The third prints another string. Each call creates a separate output line.

examples.title: Ask and greet
examples.explanation: prompt returns text. The + joins two strings. Set a response below the editor before running.

examples.title: A live text update
examples.code:
document.getElementById("message").textContent = "Hello from JavaScript!";
console.log("The preview now has new text.");
examples.explanation: The message element is found by its id, then its text is replaced. Other page elements are unchanged.

examples.title: Historical output
examples.code: document.write("Hello from an older technique");
examples.explanation: The lab simulates this as text. On real pages, document.write is generally avoided because it can replace the document and has other loading and security drawbacks.

predict.explanation: The first call prints text. The second adds two numbers before printing.

debug.hint: The opening parenthesis needs a closing partner before the semicolon.

challenge.prompt: Change the preview message to “My first program” and print 5 × 6.
challenge.starter: // Update the message, then log a calculation
challenge.hint: Use textContent for the preview and * for multiplication.

quiz.explanation: console.log is the method that writes a message to the console.
// tells JavaScript to ignore the rest of that line.
prompt returns a string, or null on cancellation. Convert numeric input explicitly.

lessons.summary: Use console.log to inspect a program. Match quotes and parentheses. Comments explain code. Use textContent to update text; avoid document.write in modern applications.

notes.say: The computer follows exactly what we write, including punctuation.
notes.demo: Run three console.log calls. Remove a quote, observe the error, then repair it.
notes.ask: What changes if we put 10 + 20 inside quotes?
notes.answer: It becomes text, so the console prints 10 + 20 instead of calculating 30.
notes.misconception: The console is not the same thing as the visible web page.
notes.exercise: Print a name, an addition, and a sentence on separate lines.
notes.transition: Programs become more useful when they can remember information.

lessons.title: Variables & data types
lessons.subtitle: Give your ideas a name. Give your program a memory.
lessons.objective: Declare variables, distinguish data types, reassign values, and convert text to numbers.
lessons.why: A program needs to remember changing information instead of repeating the same literal values everywhere.
lessons.real: A shop remembers a product name (string), price (number), and availability (boolean).
lessons.analogy: Variables are labeled storage boxes. The label is the name; the contents are the value. A const label cannot be reassigned to a different value.

sections.title: Declare once, update when needed
sections.text: A declaration introduces a name. let allows later reassignment. const requires an initial value and prevents reassignment. Prefer const when you do not need to reassign; choose let for a changing value. var is older, function-scoped, and can be redeclared; let and const are block-scoped (limited to their surrounding { } block).

sections.title: Names that explain themselves
sections.text: Use descriptive camelCase names such as studentName. Names can include letters, digits, _, and $, but cannot start with a digit or use reserved keywords. Names are case-sensitive: age and Age are different variables.

sections.title: Meet the everyday types
sections.text: A string is text in quotes. A number represents numeric values, including decimals. A boolean is true or false. undefined commonly means no value has been assigned. null is a deliberate empty value. typeof reports a type name; a historical quirk makes typeof null return "object".

sections.title: Other types, without the overwhelm
sections.text: Objects group information. Arrays are objects that hold ordered lists. Functions are callable objects. BigInt handles whole numbers beyond the safe integer range of Number; Symbol creates unique identifiers. You do not need these advanced types to complete today’s class. const does not freeze an object’s contents; it prevents replacing the variable’s value.

sections.title: Text and numbers are different
sections.text: Number("20") converts numeric text to a number. String(20) converts a number to text. Boolean(value) converts to true or false; empty string and 0 are false, but "false" and "0" are nonempty strings and therefore true. Number("hello") gives NaN, a special numeric value meaning Not a Number. Number("") gives 0, so validate empty form inputs before conversion.
sections.code:
console.log("20" + 1); // "201"
console.log(Number("20") + 1); // 21

examples.title: A student profile
examples.explanation: Each name holds a different kind of value. typeof prints string, number, and boolean.

examples.title: Update a box
examples.explanation: The right side is calculated using the old age. The result replaces the stored value.

examples.title: Convert an input
examples.explanation: Use the prompt response field for numeric text. Number converts it before addition.

predict.explanation: The left operand is a string, so + joins the string and the converted text "1".

debug.prompt: The score should be allowed to change. Fix the declaration.
debug.hint: const prevents reassignment. Which keyword allows the box to hold a new value?

challenge.prompt: Create a student profile with a name, age, and isStudent. Print each type and increase age by one.
challenge.starter: // Declare three variables, then update age
challenge.hint: Use strings for names, numbers for ages, and booleans for yes/no facts.

quiz.explanation: let allows a name to hold a new value after declaration.
Number converts valid numeric text so arithmetic works as expected.

quiz.prompt: undefined and null always mean exactly the same thing.
quiz.explanation: undefined often means not assigned; null is an intentional empty value.

lessons.summary: Use const by default and let for reassignment. Values have types. Convert input deliberately. Names are case-sensitive, and declaration is different from reassignment.

notes.say: A variable gives a value a useful name so we can remember and update it.
notes.demo: Change the age box. Lock it as const and try changing it again.
notes.ask: Is "20" the same kind of value as 20?
notes.answer: No. The quoted value is a string; the unquoted value is a number. This affects +.
notes.misconception: const prevents reassignment, not all mutation inside objects.
notes.exercise: Write a profile with a string, a number, and a boolean. Print their types.
notes.transition: Now that we can store values, let’s do something with them.

lessons.title: The operator lab
lessons.subtitle: Calculate, compare, and ask better questions.
lessons.objective: Calculate with numbers, compare values, combine boolean conditions, and understand equality.
lessons.why: Stored values are useful when we can transform them or ask questions about them.
lessons.real: A checkout calculates a bill, a scoreboard compares results, and a form combines several validation checks.
lessons.analogy: Arithmetic operators are calculator keys. Comparison operators are questions whose answers are true or false.

sections.title: Arithmetic and order
sections.text: + adds numbers, - subtracts, * multiplies, / divides, % gives the remainder, and ** raises a number to a power. Multiplication and division happen before addition and subtraction; parentheses make order explicit. Dividing a nonzero number by zero yields Infinity; 0 / 0 yields NaN.
sections.code:
console.log(2 + 3 * 4); // 14
console.log((2 + 3) * 4); // 20
console.log(7 % 2); // 1

sections.title: Assignment changes a value
sections.text: = assigns a value. += adds and assigns; -= subtracts and assigns. ++ increases by one and -- decreases by one. In a standalone statement, score++ updates score. Inside a larger expression, postfix score++ returns the old value; prefix ++score returns the new one.

sections.title: Comparison asks a question
sections.text: >, <, >=, and <= compare values. === checks equality without converting types; !== checks strict inequality. == and != can convert types first. Prefer strict equality for predictable beginner code. = is assignment and should not be confused with ===.
sections.code:
console.log(5 === "5"); // false
console.log(5 == "5");  // true
console.log(5 !== 3);   // true

sections.title: Combine yes/no answers
sections.text: && means AND, || means OR, and ! means NOT. With boolean operands, AND is true only when both are true; OR is true when at least one is true. NOT flips truthiness. In general, && and || return an operand and short-circuit (stop when the result is decided), so use boolean expressions for clear beginner decisions.

examples.title: A shopping bill
examples.explanation: Multiplication calculates the item total, then delivery is added: 490.

examples.title: Exam percentage
examples.explanation: Divide by the maximum, then multiply by 100. A comparison produces a boolean.

examples.title: Even numbers and higher scores
examples.explanation: Even integers leave a remainder of zero when divided by two.

predict.explanation: 3 * 4 happens first, then 2 is added. Parentheses would change the order.

debug.prompt: The bill joins text instead of adding. Convert the input before adding delivery.
debug.hint: The + operator joins when one value is a string. Number() can convert the price.

challenge.prompt: A notebook costs 60. Buy 4 and add 25 delivery. Print the bill and whether it is greater than 250.
challenge.hint: Store the total first, then compare that total to 250.

quiz.prompt: Which checks equality without converting types?
quiz.explanation: === compares without type coercion. = assigns; == may convert types.

quiz.prompt: Both a ticket AND an open gate are required. Choose the operator.
quiz.explanation: AND requires both boolean conditions to be true.
The remainder operator gives zero when an integer divides evenly by two.

lessons.summary: Arithmetic transforms values. Comparisons return booleans. = assigns, === compares. Use parentheses for clarity and && / || to combine conditions.

notes.say: Some operators calculate answers. Others ask questions.
notes.demo: Move a and b in the operator lab; make them equal, then set b to zero.
notes.answer: The values have different types, and strict equality does not convert them.
notes.misconception: = does not ask whether two values are equal.
notes.exercise: Calculate a snack bill and check whether it exceeds a budget.
notes.transition: A true or false answer can now choose which instruction happens next.

lessons.title: Decisions & conditions
lessons.subtitle: Teach your program to choose its next move.
lessons.objective: Use if, else if, else, nested conditions, and switch to choose a branch.
lessons.why: A program must respond differently to different situations instead of executing every possible action.
lessons.real: An app can show a pass message for one score and a retry message for another. Server-side checks must still enforce access and validate important decisions.
lessons.analogy: Conditions are decision gates. At a gate, a yes/no question sends you down one path.

sections.title: The first gate: if and else
sections.text: A condition is an expression evaluated for truthiness. if runs its block when the condition is truthy. else runs when it is falsy. true and false are booleans; other values have truthiness too. 0, "", null, undefined, and NaN are falsy. Braces group instructions into a block.

sections.title: More than two choices
sections.text: else if checks another condition only if earlier checks failed. The first matching branch wins. Order matters: check high grade thresholds before lower ones. In this lab, A is 90–100, B is 75–89, C is 60–74, D is 40–59, and below 40 means retry.

sections.title: A decision inside a decision
sections.text: A nested condition is an if inside another if. It is useful when a second question only matters after the first is answered. Keep nesting shallow so the code is easy to follow.

sections.title: switch for fixed choices
sections.text: switch compares an expression to each case using strict equality. break exits the switch; without it, execution falls through to later cases. default handles unmatched choices. if is convenient for ranges; switch is convenient for discrete values.

sections.title: Optional: the ternary shortcut
sections.text: condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse chooses between two values. Use it for simple choices. Common mistakes include using = inside a condition, putting a semicolon immediately after if (...), or forgetting braces around multiple statements.

examples.title: Traffic controller
examples.explanation: Exactly one matching branch prints its message. Try red, yellow, and an unknown color.

examples.title: Grade a result
examples.explanation: Validate the range first, then test the thresholds in descending order.

examples.title: A mock login
examples.explanation: Both comparisons must be true. Real authentication needs secure server-side verification and must not expose passwords in client code.

predict.explanation: 82 is below 90, but at least 75. The second branch runs and later branches are skipped.

debug.prompt: This code overwrites age rather than comparing it. Make it check strict equality.
debug.hint: A single = assigns. Use three equals signs to compare without type conversion.

challenge.prompt: Give a 10% discount when a cart total is at least 1000. Print the final payable amount.
challenge.hint: Multiplying by 0.9 leaves 90% of the original total.

quiz.prompt: How many branches run in one if / else if / else chain?
quiz.explanation: The first matching branch runs. The rest of the chain is skipped.

quiz.prompt: What can happen without break in a switch case?
quiz.explanation: Execution continues into following cases until a break or the end of the switch.

quiz.prompt: Which is clearest for checking a range of marks?
quiz.explanation: Comparisons such as marks >= 75 naturally fit an if / else if chain.

lessons.summary: Conditions select branches. Check ranges with if / else if, discrete cases with switch, and combine checks with logical operators. Validate input before making decisions.

notes.say: The computer does not guess. We define a question and the instruction for each answer.
notes.demo: Try marks 74, 75, 89, and 90 to show exact boundaries.
notes.ask: What happens if we check marks >= 40 before marks >= 90?
notes.answer: A score of 95 matches the first check, so the chain stops too early.
notes.misconception: Client-side demo credentials are not secure authentication.
notes.exercise: Write an age check with one message for 18 or older and another for younger ages.
notes.transition: We can choose instructions. Next, we’ll repeat them without copying the same line.

lessons.title: Loops & repetition
lessons.subtitle: Write it once. Make it happen again and again.
lessons.objective: Trace for, while, and do…while loops; control repetition with break and continue.
lessons.why: Repeating the same instruction manually is slow and error-prone. A loop describes what repeats and when it stops.
lessons.real: A shop can process each cart item, a game can count down, and a classroom tool can generate a multiplication table.
lessons.analogy: A loop is a repeated instruction like “give each student a worksheet.” The condition asks whether there are students left.

sections.title: A for loop has three controls
sections.text: Initialization runs once. The condition is checked before each iteration (one pass through the body). If true, the body runs, then the update runs. If false, execution leaves the loop. With i from 1 through 5, the final check is 6 <= 5, which is false.

sections.title: while: check, then repeat
sections.text: while checks its condition before every iteration. It may run zero times. Choose for when the counting pattern is clear; choose while when repetition depends on a changing condition. Remember to change something that eventually makes the condition false.

sections.title: do…while: do it at least once
sections.text: do…while runs the body before checking the condition, so it always runs at least once. Notice the semicolon after the final condition.

sections.title: Skip or stop
sections.text: continue skips the rest of the current iteration. In a for loop, the update still runs. break exits the nearest loop immediately. In a while loop, an update placed after continue may be skipped and cause an infinite loop.

sections.title: Optional: a loop inside a loop
sections.text: Nested loops repeat one complete inner loop for every outer iteration. They can draw rows and columns. Large nested loops do a lot of work. A missing update, a condition that never becomes false, or the wrong direction can create an infinite loop. Our visual simulator caps the limit at 20 and our code runner terminates after one second.

examples.title: Count from 1 to 10
examples.explanation: There are ten successful condition checks, ten prints, and one final false check.

examples.title: Even numbers from 1 to 20
examples.explanation: Odd numbers skip the print. The update still runs after continue.

examples.title: A multiplication table
examples.explanation: i changes each time; number stays the same.

examples.title: Sum and countdown
examples.explanation: An accumulator stores a running total. A countdown uses a decreasing value.

predict.explanation: i takes 1, 2, 3, and 4. When i becomes 5, i < 5 is false.

debug.prompt: This loop never changes i. Repair it before running.
debug.hint: Update the counter inside the body so the condition eventually becomes false.

challenge.prompt: Print numbers 1 to 10, skip 3, and stop before printing 8.
challenge.hint: Use continue for 3 and break for 8, before console.log.

quiz.prompt: Which loop always runs its body at least once?
quiz.explanation: do…while checks after the body, so the first pass happens even if the condition is false.

quiz.prompt: Skip only the current iteration using ___.
quiz.explanation: continue skips the rest of the current body. break would leave the loop entirely.

quiz.prompt: A while loop condition stays true forever. What is likely missing?
choices: A string quote in every number
quiz.explanation: A loop must eventually change something that makes its condition false, or use break.

lessons.summary: Initialize, check, run the body, update, and repeat. for and while check first; do…while checks after. continue skips a pass, break stops the loop. Always plan a stopping condition.

notes.say: A loop is a question we keep asking, with an instruction between each answer.
notes.demo: Step through all five prints and the final false condition. Go backward to compare the state.
notes.ask: When the loop finishes, is the last checked value 5 or 6?
notes.answer: 6. The update after printing 5 changes i to 6, and the next condition is false.
notes.misconception: The last printed value and the final checked counter are not necessarily the same.
notes.exercise: Print five even numbers, then change the loop to count backward.
notes.transition: You can now remember, calculate, choose, and repeat. Combine those tools in a small project.

arena.prompt: Choose a variable that can be reassigned.
arena.explanation: let supports reassignment, making it suitable for a changing score.
One operand is a string, so + concatenates the values.

arena.prompt: Convert user input to a number with ___.
arena.explanation: Number converts numeric text into a numeric value for arithmetic.
Strict equality does not convert types. A number and a string differ.

arena.prompt: You need a ticket AND an open gate. Use ___.
arena.explanation: Both conditions are required, which is logical AND.
40 >= 40 is true, so the first branch runs.
= assigns. Use === to ask whether age equals 18.

arena.prompt: What is the last printed number?
arena.explanation: i starts at 1, prints through 3, then becomes 4 and fails the condition.

arena.prompt: Leave the nearest loop immediately with ___.
arena.explanation: break exits the loop. continue skips only the current iteration.
